No. 25A693
________________________________________
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
________________________________________
FRANK A. WALLS,
Petitioner,
vs.
STATE OF FLORIDA,
Respondent.
________________________________________________________
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO THE
FLORIDA SUPREME COURT
_____________________________________________________________
REPLY TO RESPONSE APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
______________________________________________________________
CAPITAL CASE
DEATH WARRANT SIGNED
Execution Scheduled: December 18, 2025, at 6:00 p.m.
______________________________________________________________
REPLY TO RESPONSE FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
The State filed its Brief in Opposition this afternoon and raised several 
arguments based on Hamm v. Smith, SC 24-872, which is pending a decision before 
this Court and had oral arguments conducted last week. The State’s arguments raise 
further issues that tie the issues and questions raised in Mr. Walls’ Petition for a

2
Writ of Certiorari to that litigation. As a result Mr. Walls requests that this Court 
stay the execution of Mr. Walls until Hamm v. Smith, SC 24-872 is decided.
The underlying issues present significant, compelling questions of 
constitutional law and a stay is necessary to avoid Walls being executed in violation 
of the Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution. It is indisputable Walls
will be irreparably harmed if his execution is allowed to go forward, and the balance 
of equities weighs heavily in favor of a stay. Especially since the State of Florida feels 
that the pending litigation in Hamm v. Smith has direct bearing on Mr. Walls’ case. 
It would be in the best interest to resolve the matter along with Hamm.
Florida’s interest in the timely enforcement of judgments handed down by its 
courts must be weighed against Walls’ continued interest in his life. See Ohio Adult 
Parole Auth. v. Woodard, 523 U.S. 272, 289 (1998) (“[I]t is incorrect . . . to say that a 
prisoner has been deprived of all interest in his life before his execution.”)(O’Connor, 
J., plurality opinion). Florida has a minimal interest in finality and efficient 
enforcement of judgments, while Walls has a right and significant interest in 
ensuring that his execution comports with the Constitution. In addition, the 
irreversible nature of the death penalty supports granting a stay. “[A] death sentence 
cannot begin to be carried out by the State while substantial legal issues remain 
outstanding.” Barefoot, 463 U.S. at 888. Should this Court grant the request for a 
stay and review of the underlying petition, Walls submits there is a significant 
possibility of the lower court’s reversal. This Court’s intervention is urgently needed 
to prevent Pittman’s imminent execution despite the protections from the death

3
penalty provided by the Eighth Amendment. Specifically, the State of Florida runs 
the imminent risk of executing an intellectually disabled person, contrary to the 
provisions of the Eighth Amendment.
Walls’ case presents two significant constitutional issues, which need to be 
fully addressed by this Court free from the extreme time constraints set by the 
warrant signed on November 18, 2025. Walls’ execution is scheduled for December 
18, 2025. Walls respectfully requests this Court enter a stay of execution.
As detailed in Walls’ contemporaneous petition for writ of certiorari, due to 
Florida’s erroneous interpretation of federal law, and its insistence on placing a time 
bar on intellectual disability claims, the State of Florida will execute an intellectually 
disabled defendant, in violation of the United States Constitution. Mr. Walls, due to 
the arbitrary bars and changing interpretation of federal law by the Florida’s 
Supreme Court, Mr. Walls, a man with a significant history of intellectual disability 
will be executed. Further Mr. Walls was denied due process by being unable to fully 
demonstrate and prove his intellectual disability contrary to Atkins v. Virginia, 536 
U.S. 304, 321 (2002) and its progeny.
CONCLUSION
“The fundamental requirement of due process is the opportunity to be heard 
‘at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.’” Armstrong v. Manzo, 380 U.S. 
545, 552 (1965). Windom’s meritorious issues cannot possibly be heard in a 
meaningful manner with just days left until his execution. The important

4
constitutional issues presented by Walls’ case require a full appellate review that is 
not truncated by his imminent execution. 
For the foregoing reasons, Walls respectfully requests that this Court grant his 
application for a stay of Walls’ execution scheduled for December 18, 2025, to address 
the compelling constitutional questions in his case on the merits.
Respectfully submitted,
